newsitem.title: USA: Californians weigh future of affirmative action.
newsitem.headline: Californians weigh future of affirmative action.

text.p: Californians may strike a blow at 30 years of U.S. policy when they vote next month on a proposal to ban state affirmative action programmes giving preferential treatment to women and minorities.

The California Civil Rights Initiative, also known as Proposition 209, is the most explosive issue to be decided by voters in the nation's most ethnically diverse state in the Nov. 5 election. Written by two academics, it would ban state and local government affirmative action programmes in public employment, education and contracting in California that are based on race or sex.

The vote will be closely watched in other states and could influence the future of affirmative action programmes around the country that have been used since the 1960s to expand opportunities for women and racial minorities.

Supporters of the measure say race and gender preferences are unfair and may discriminate against someone who is better qualified. Opponents say minorities and women still face discrimination in education and the workplace and affirmative action is needed to "level the playing field."

Ward Connerly, a black Sacramento businessman and chairman of the California Civil Rights Initiative, says Californians are obsessed with race. "It's time ... for us to get beyond it and we are not going to get beyond it as long as our government agencies classify us and decide who gets a job and who gets a contract ... on the basis of their race," he said.

"I think we have reached the point in California where we should not presume that all black people are by definition disadvantaged or all Hispanics are disadvantaged by definition," he told a news conference.

But Lulann McGriff, a northern California official of the National Association for the Advancement of Coloured People, calling the measure deceptive and mean-spirited, said it would have "a devastating effect." There was still discrimination in jobs, housing and education, she said. "Anyone who has been of a minority in this country can certainly attest to that."

A poll by the independent Field Institute this month found 47 percent of likely voters supporting Proposition 209 and 32 percent against, although support has fallen in recent months. Opponents hope to sway voters with a television advertising campaign in the next two weeks.

The measure is on the ballot two years after another controversial measure passed in California. The 1994 initiative, which would cut off services to illegal immigrants, has been tied up in the courts ever since.

If it passes, Proposition 209 would eliminate California programmes that give preference to women-owned or minority-owned companies on public contracts, the state legislative analyst's office said. It would also stop the state university's practice of using race as a factor in some admissions decisions and it could eliminate voluntary desegregation programmes run by school districts.

President Bill Clinton, who opposes the California measure, and Republican challenger Bob Dole, who supports it, argued over affirmative action and the California initiative in their debate in San Diego last week.

"I have never supported quotas ... but I do favour making sure everybody has a chance to prove they're competent," Clinton said after Dole spoke out against preferences and quotas. But affirmative action has not turned into the key presidential issue that some expected it to be because, political analysts say, it is too much of a "hot potato."
